general: The forest of Fangorn is ancient beyond the reckoning of men; its trees were old when Gondor was young and the sea was narrow.
In Lothlórien time moves differently; the golden mallorn leaves drift through air that smells of something older and purer than the outside world.
Mirkwood closes around the path like a dark hand, and those who stray from the trail find themselves turned around and lost beyond recovery.
The Ents move slowly because they have learned that haste is a mistake, and they have the memories of trees to learn it from.
There are voices in old forests that have no speakers you can see, and whether they mean you well or ill depends on how you listen.
Galadriel's wood was a place outside of time, where travellers found themselves rested and haunted in equal measure.
The trees of Fangorn remember the wars of the First Age; they carry grievances older than the kingdoms of men.
In the heart of the old forest, even a wizard might feel young and uncertain, for the oldest things alive look through you rather than at you.
The light in Lothlórien comes from the trees themselves; no torch or fire is needed here, and none would feel appropriate.
Treebeard's voice was like a long, slow creak of ancient timber, and it carried the weight of centuries in every syllable.
Do not enter the Old Forest after dark — this is advice given by those who have done so and been fortunate enough to return.
The Ent-draught tasted of the deep soil and long rain and sunlit centuries, and those who drank it felt themselves grow in some indefinable way.
gandalf: The oldest forests are archives; they remember what no book has recorded and no scholar has the patience to ask.
I have spoken with the trees of Fangorn, and their anger at the deforestation of Isengard is something I would not wish to be on the receiving end of.
Even I do not know all the names of the things that dwell in the deep places of Fangorn; some things are older than my knowledge.
legolas: The trees here are alive with more than sap and chlorophyll; they carry memories and intentions, and I would not want to offend them.
I could hear the mallorns singing as we entered Lothlórien, and for a moment I forgot everything dark that lay outside its borders.
Elves and trees have an understanding that goes beyond words; we feel the age of them and they feel the grief in us.
gimli: I am not fond of forests, as a rule; you cannot see what is coming, the footing is treacherous, and everything looks the same.
That said, even I could feel something in Lothlórien that my hammer could not quantify and my axe could not address.
Trees are fine in their place, but underground — now that's where you can really appreciate the architecture.
frodo: The Fellowship rested in Lothlórien and I dreamed there, or perhaps did not dream, and I was not sure which was more frightening.
There is a comfort in old forests, even dark ones — they were here before the trouble started and they will be here when it ends.
sam: I've never seen trees like these, Mr. Frodo — they seem to be watching us, and not all of them seem pleased about what they're seeing.
Elvish rope and elvish bread and elvish rope — I'll say this for the elves, they make things that last.
